A strong software business hasn't been enough to offset a stalled consulting arm at IBM (NYSE:IBM) this year. IBM stock is down 21% year to date (YTD) to $231.81 in late-day trading. Broad technology selling is adding a 4% decline to that slide.

MajestiX B / Shutterstock.com

Starting 2026 at $288.30, IBM stock spent part of the year above the $250 level. Over the past 52 weeks, IBM has traded between $196.41 and $327.83. Getting back to that round number may take faster consulting growth and continued software momentum at the company.

IBM Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
What Dragged IBM Lower in 2026

The turning point came on July 22, when IBM reported Q2 2026 operating diluted earnings per share (EPS) of $2.93, missing the $2.97 consensus and ending a five-quarter beat streak. Management cited "revenue headwinds late in the second quarter," and IBM Z mainframe revenue fell 42% as the product cycle aged.

IBM's next report on October 21 told a better story. The company posted its Q3 2026 adjusted EPS of $2.95 against a $2.87 consensus, while its revenue rose 4.7% year over year (YoY) to $17.10 billion. CEO Arvind Krishna said "Transaction processing grew 10%, underscoring the strategic importance of the mainframe and validating our view that the softness we saw in the second quarter reflected timing rather than underlying demand."

Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) trades at $119.05. Wall Street's average price target is $236.18, suggesting about 98% of potential gain.

Justin Sullivan / Getty Images

Oracle has turned itself from a database and license vendor into a large AI cloud provider. Cloud now makes up 60% of revenue, and cloud infrastructure revenue grew 121% last quarter. Remaining performance obligations (RPO), the backlog of contracted revenue Oracle hasn't recognized yet, reached $664B.

Oracle keeps beating estimates while its stock keeps falling. That leaves two options. Analysts may be holding onto a story the market has given up on, or the market may be mispricing the stock.

Oracle Beat Earnings Estimates and Still Fell 35.73% in Six Months

Cash burn is the main reason for the selloff. Oracle spent $28.5B on capex last quarter, so free cash flow came in at negative $5.40B. Management hasn't given a timeline for positive free cash flow. To pay for the expansion, Oracle finished a $20B at-the-market equity program and then priced another $20 billion of common stock and senior notes. That means shareholders face dilution and rising interest costs together (the same power, cooling, and networking suppliers riding this AI data-center spend are the subject of a free report we put together, here).

According to Bloomberg, Goldman Sachs and Apollo Global Management are expected to underwrite the offering.

Funds associated with BlackRock and KKR have also made financing commitments

Microsoft, Meta and Oracle recently announced plans to raise funds for AI expansion.

SpaceX (SPCX) could begin selling bonds worth around $4 billion this week as part of its $40 billion financing plan to expand its AI computing business.

According to a Bloomberg report on Tuesday, Goldman Sachs (GS) and Apollo Global Management (APO) are expected to be the underwriters of the sale.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

SPCX shares were up 2.9% at the time of writing.

SPCX's $40B Financing To Buy Nvidia's Vera Rubin chips

In October, SpaceX announced a $40 billion financing commitment to acquire Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin chips for its computing infrastructure. Under the proposed arrangement, a special-purpose company managed by Apollo-backed Atlas SP will purchase the chips and lease them to SpaceX for five years.

Funds associated with BlackRock (BLK) and KKR (KKR) also made financing commitments.

The structure is designed to keep the borrowing off SpaceX's balance sheet and protect its investment-grade credit ratings, the report read.

At the time of writing, SpaceX had not responded to Stocktwits' request for a comment on the Bloomberg report.

Big Tech Turns To Bonds For AI Expansion

SpaceX's financing plans come amid a wave of borrowing by major technology companies to fund expensive AI infrastructure projects. Last month, Microsoft (MSFT) announced a $25 billion bond offering, its first U.S. debt sale since 2017.

Meanwhile, Oracle (ORCL) announced plans to sell $10 billion in bonds earlier this month, alongside a roughly $10 billion stock offering, to support its AI and cloud expansion. Meta Platforms is also reportedly targeting at least $20 billion in a multi-currency investment-grade bond deal to fund its ongoing operations and capital needs.

Last week, Wells Fargo said that heavy borrowing in the technology sector is beginning to strain investor demand for corporate bonds.

Retail Remains 'Bullish' On SPCX

Retail sentiment surrounding SPCX on Stocktwits remained 'bullish' over the past 24 hours.

SPCX shares have gained 4.5% so far in 2026.

On Adobe, Burry said he bought near $246 and believes the company can adapt to artificial intelligence. He noted that free alternatives to Photoshop have existed for decades, yet Adobe has grown revenue by at least 10% in each of the past four years.

The Oracle and Caterpillar trades were put options, contracts that gain value when a stock falls. Burry cited continued declines in both shares.

He still holds a large put position in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH), along with puts on the Nasdaq 100, Nvidia (NVDA), MetLife (NYSE:MET) and Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR).

On November 16, Burry said he had sold his Oracle puts, options that gain value when a stock falls. His reasoning centered on cost and portfolio balance. He noted his overall put book "continues to grow in size, so trimming made sense," and added that "puts, with the higher volatility of late, are getting expensive." The investor is now considering outright short sales instead.

Burry still holds puts on the NASDAQ 100, a semiconductor exchange-traded fund and several AI-linked stocks.
